// Code generated by go-bindings-codegen. DO NOT EDIT.

//go:build darwin

// Package errkit holds the error and panic types the generated Go APIs use to
// report Objective-C failures.
//
// Objective-C reports problems two different ways, and this package maps each to
// the matching Go idiom:
//
//   - An NSError signals an expected, recoverable failure (a file is missing, a
//     network call failed). The generated code returns it as a Go error backed
//     by [*Error], which you can inspect or compare.
//   - An NSException signals a programming mistake (an index out of range). The
//     generated code panics with an [*Exception], matching how Go itself panics
//     on misuse such as indexing a slice out of bounds.
//
// [Error] gives you the failure's domain and numeric code plus the
// human-readable messages, and works with errors.Is and errors.As. Each
// framework package also declares named error values (built with [New]) so you
// can test for a specific failure with errors.Is(err, framework.ErrSomething).
package errkit

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"unsafe"

	"github.com/deploymenttheory/go-bindings-macosplatform/bindings/runtime/purego/objcerrors"
)

// Error is the idiomatic error returned by every fallible idiomatic call.
//
// Domain and Code together are the stable, machine-readable identity of the
// error; the string fields are for display. Use errors.As to read fields and
// errors.Is (against a generated sentinel) to test identity.
type Error struct {
	domain             string
	code               int
	description        string
	failureReason      string
	recoverySuggestion string
	underlying         error
}

// New constructs a sentinel Error identified by domain and code. Generated
// per-framework error sentinels are package-level vars built with New, e.g.
//
//	var ErrNotSupported = errkit.New("VZErrorDomain", 8)
func New(domain string, code int) *Error {
	return &Error{domain: domain, code: code}
}

// Domain returns the error domain (e.g. "VZErrorDomain").
func (e *Error) Domain() string { return e.domain }

// Code returns the numeric error code within the domain.
func (e *Error) Code() int { return e.code }

// Description returns the primary human-readable message (localizedDescription).
func (e *Error) Description() string { return e.description }

// FailureReason returns a more specific explanation of why the operation
// failed (localizedFailureReason), or "" if none was supplied.
func (e *Error) FailureReason() string { return e.failureReason }

// RecoverySuggestion returns what could be done to resolve the error
// (localizedRecoverySuggestion), or "" if none was supplied.
func (e *Error) RecoverySuggestion() string { return e.recoverySuggestion }

// Error implements the error interface.
func (e *Error) Error() string {
	if e.description == "" {
		return fmt.Sprintf("[%s:%d]", e.domain, e.code)
	}
	s := fmt.Sprintf("[%s:%d] %s", e.domain, e.code, e.description)
	if e.failureReason != "" {
		s += " — " + e.failureReason
	}
	if e.recoverySuggestion != "" {
		s += " (" + e.recoverySuggestion + ")"
	}
	return s
}

// Unwrap returns the underlying cause, or nil. This lets errors.Is / errors.As
// traverse the NSError underlying-error chain.
func (e *Error) Unwrap() error { return e.underlying }

// Is reports whether target identifies the same error kind, matching on domain
// and code. This is what makes errors.Is(err, sentinel) work against a
// generated sentinel built with [New].
func (e *Error) Is(target error) bool {
	t, ok := target.(*Error)
	if !ok {
		return false
	}
	return t.domain == e.domain && t.code == e.code
}

// FromObjC turns an error that came from converting an Objective-C NSError into
// an [*Error]. It returns nil for a nil error, and returns the error unchanged
// if it did not originate from an NSError. The generated code calls this so the
// errors it returns are always the [*Error] type documented here.
func FromObjC(err error) error {
	if err == nil {
		return nil
	}
	var oe *objcerrors.ObjCError
	if errors.As(err, &oe) && oe != nil {
		return fromObjCError(oe)
	}
	return err
}

// FromCFError converts a CoreFoundation error reference (the value written to a
// CFErrorRef out-parameter) into an idiomatic error. It returns nil when ptr is
// nil (no error occurred).
func FromCFError(ptr unsafe.Pointer) error {
	if ptr == nil {
		return nil
	}
	return FromObjC(objcerrors.CFErrorToError(ptr))
}

func fromObjCError(oe *objcerrors.ObjCError) *Error {
	e := &Error{
		domain:             oe.Domain,
		code:               int(oe.Code),
		description:        oe.Description,
		failureReason:      oe.FailureReason,
		recoverySuggestion: oe.RecoverySuggestion,
	}
	if len(oe.Underlying) > 0 && oe.Underlying[0] != nil {
		e.underlying = fromObjCError(oe.Underlying[0])
	}
	return e
}

// Exception is the value a generated method panics with when it detects a
// programming mistake — such as an out-of-range index — before calling into
// Objective-C. Panicking here matches how Go itself behaves when you index a
// slice out of range, and it avoids a lower-level crash inside Objective-C.
type Exception struct {
	// Name is the Objective-C exception name, e.g. "NSRangeException".
	Name string
	// Reason is a human-readable explanation of the misuse.
	Reason string
}

// Error implements the error interface so a recovered Exception can be handled
// as an error if desired.
func (e *Exception) Error() string {
	if e.Reason == "" {
		return e.Name
	}
	return e.Name + ": " + e.Reason
}

// CheckIndex panics with an [*Exception] when index is outside the range
// [0, length), just as indexing a Go slice out of range would. Generated
// element accessors call it before reading from a collection.
func CheckIndex(index, length int) {
	if index < 0 || index >= length {
		panic(&Exception{
			Name:   "NSRangeException",
			Reason: fmt.Sprintf("index %d beyond bounds [0, %d)", index, length),
		})
	}
}
